Draft Recruiting, Heather Davies Skip to content H Home W Work P Places A About Resumé ↗ ← Back Overview Impact Key Features AI Experience Components Library Draft Recruiting Modernizing a hiring pipeline with AI 3 min read ♥ 0 — Hiring used to be slow, expensive, and time-consuming. Traditional recruiting workflows were outdated and difficult to navigate, costing organizations millions in hiring expenses while slowing down the search for talent. I redesigned the experience end to end, introducing an AI-powered recruiting agent that streamlines candidate screening, automates interviews, and makes finding and hiring the right people faster and more intuitive with Draft. Role Lead Product Designer Years 2025–2026 Scope Workflow design, interface design, interaction prototyping, branding Your browser does not support HTML video. Challenge With no dedicated researchers, I had to learn and understand complex hiring workflows before redesigning anything. The challenge was to speed up candidate screening and interviews, saving time and money on hiring without sacrificing the human judgment essential to finding the right talent. Impact 486 Candidates screened annually 218 Monthly workspace visits 97.2 hrs Annual screening time saved $430 Annual net cost savings Collaboration As lead product designer, I collaborated directly with business stakeholders, PMs, and engineers from vision through execution, keeping design aligned with business goals and technical feasibility at every step. I also owned the research myself, ensuring the redesign was grounded in real user workflows rather than assumptions. Key Features Hiring Dashboard → An overview of open roles, applicant counts, and recent activity helps recruiters see what needs attention. Candidate Pipeline → Search, role filters, and hiring-stage tabs help recruiters organize applicants and find candidate records quickly. AI Interview Setup & Preparation → Recruiters configure interview questions, while candidates review instructions, check their microphone, and practice before starting. CRM → Recruiters organize talent pools, manage candidate relationships, and launch outreach campaigns from one connected CRM workspace. Purpose-Built AI Experience Draft’s scorecards bring individual interviewer evaluations together with an AI-generated summary of candidate feedback. The summary highlights recurring strengths, areas of concern, and observations across key attributes, helping recruiters understand the overall assessment without reading every scorecard separately. Interviewers’ original ratings and comments remain available so hiring teams can review the evidence behind the summary and make the final decision themselves. 05 / COMPONENTS Build consistency into the details. Navigation with clear state Underlined top tabs, selected sidebar items, and a consistent Back pattern make location visible across the workspace. Progressive disclosure Expandable filters, setup navigation, candidate panels, and stage sections keep secondary details available on demand. Editable records Hiring-team assignments, job details, openings, and candidate information use contextual controls and local saving. Semantic feedback Green identifies open status and referrals; purple marks interaction; recommendation and task states use explicit labels alongside color. 06 / PROTOTYPE LIBRARY Follow the experience. Heather Davies Design Skip to content H Home W Work P Places A About Resumé ↗ BOSTON CHILDREN’S HOSPITAL / HEALTHCARE UX A clearer path to ALS care resources. A guided web app helping people with ALS and clinicians find practical resources for communication and care. Illustrative prototype mockup of a communication resource and a save-to-folder screen · Open image at full size My role UX/UI design, research, and prototyping Focus Information architecture, resource organization, and accessibility Status Design concept and prototype The task: move from a question to a useful resource The project explores how people with ALS and clinicians can find resources through a guided series of questions. Earlier project materials describe a web app that connects answers to relevant recommendations and resources maintained by ALS experts. My design work explored how to find, save, organize, and share those resources. The current project materials describe the intended workflow and feature set. They do not document measured delays, a research sample, or clinical outcomes. Organizing the experience around three tasks 01 / Find relevant information A guided survey is proposed as a route to relevant resources. It offers more direction than an undifferentiated list, but introduces questions before the user reaches content. A next test should compare this approach with direct browsing. 02 / Save resources for later Folders and bookmarking support repeated access. The concept includes creating, renaming, moving, sharing, and deleting folders. The design question is whether this level of organization helps clinicians retrieve information or adds unnecessary management work. 03 / Share a resource with a colleague Sharing completes the proposed workflow. The final interaction, permissions, and delivery method need to be confirmed before presenting a production-ready handoff. A proposed task walkthrough This sequence describes the concept; it is not a tested interactive prototype. Find Use the guided survey or browse available resource categories. Save Bookmark a relevant resource and organize it in a folder. Share Choose the information to pass to another clinician. The image above is an illustrative redesign concept. An interaction recording would provide a fuller view of how the flow works. Exploring more communication resources These illustrative concepts explore how resource pages could introduce partner-assisted scanning and message banking. The content and interactions would need review with ALS communication specialists and users. AI-assisted illustrative resource concepts Accessibility as a requirement to verify The concept proposes text-size and weight controls, color choices, and contrast adjustment. These preferences should complement a usable default experience. A next review should check keyboard navigation, visible focus, semantic headings, screen-reader labels, contrast, and text reflow. The materials shown here do not establish that these checks have been completed. Intended benefits and an evaluation plan The intended benefits are easier resource discovery and less repeated searching. These remain design goals, rather than demonstrated improvements in clinical decisions. Findability: Ask clinicians to locate a specified resource; observe completion, time, and wrong turns. Retrieval: Ask them to return to a saved item and compare folders with a simpler saved list. Sharing: Check whether recipients and shared content are clear before the action is completed. Accessibility: Pair interface checks with testing by people who use assistive technology. ← Selected work Chaos & Order → Heather Davies © 2026 A more curious life. Work About Resumé

SIGNAL — Heather Davies Design Skip to content H Home W Work P Places A About Resumé ↗ SIGNAL / PRODUCT DESIGN CONCEPT A clearer path to what’s next. A job search workspace that brings applications, interview details, and follow-ups into one place. Illustrative interface concept · Example companies, people, and application data Discipline Product design & visual systems Scope Application tracking, job details, and follow-ups Status Concept with an early browser-based version The challenge A job search involves more than sending applications. Each opportunity carries a different status, contact, deadline, and next step. When those details live across tabs, emails, and notes, it can be difficult to see what needs attention. SIGNAL explores a focused workspace for keeping that information connected. The guiding design question: how might a job seeker understand their pipeline and choose their next action without rebuilding the context each time? A workspace organized around momentum The concept moves from a broad view of the search to the details of one opportunity, then to the timing of the next action. Track See applications grouped by stage. Prepare Open an opportunity and review its details. Follow through Review upcoming interviews and follow-ups. Three decisions that shaped the experience 01 / Make application stages visible The board groups opportunities into Applied, Screening, Interview, Offer, and Not Moving Forward. Keeping the stages side by side makes the current state of the search visible without opening every application. Summary counts support a quick scan, while individual cards retain company and role context. The trade-off is density: a long pipeline will need filtering and an accessible list alternative. 02 / Keep the opportunity’s context together The detail view brings the role, company, application information, and related actions into one place. This gives the job seeker a place to return before an interview or follow-up. The hierarchy prioritizes the current opportunity over general navigation. Contact, document, and note areas are directions shown in the visual concept; their full interactions remain to be developed. 03 / Connect progress to a next step A calendar pairs upcoming events with a monthly view. The intent is to help users move from knowing an application’s stage to knowing when something needs to happen. The next iteration should make action labels, due dates, and overdue states explicit, with text and icons supporting color cues. A calm visual system for a busy process A restrained green accent distinguishes selected navigation and key actions. Neutral surfaces, compact cards, and consistent spacing keep the interface organized as the number of applications grows. The visual direction balances an overview with readable detail. Keyboard access, focus states, contrast, and narrow-screen layouts still need verification. From concept to an early tool The existing browser-based first version supports adding applications with a stage, next step, and follow-up date, then reviewing or removing saved entries. Entries are stored in the current browser; editing an existing entry is not yet supported. The richer board, detail, and calendar screens shown above explore the intended product direction beyond that initial tool. Try the early version ↗ What I would test next The design has not yet been validated through user testing. A first study would focus on three practical tasks: Find the next action: identify an application that needs a follow-up and explain why. Update an opportunity: move an application to a new stage and check that the change is clear. Prepare for an interview: locate the event, role details, and relevant notes. I would observe task completion, missed information, and confusion between application status and scheduled events. Those findings would guide changes before adding more features. Reflection SIGNAL’s central idea is to make a job search easier to resume. The strongest next step is to test whether this structure helps people act with less searching and re-reading. The current work establishes a visual direction and a starting workflow; measured outcomes are still ahead. ← Selected work Talentora Interviewing → Heather Davies © 2026 A more curious life.
